authorities.proposition: Section 1983 supplies a civil action against a person who, under color of state law, causes the deprivation of a right secured by the Constitution or federal law; it does not itself define the Fourth Amendment force standard or eliminate a properly established immunity defense.

Force used during a seizure is judged for objective reasonableness under the Fourth Amendment from the perspective of an officer on the scene, considering the circumstances of the particular encounter rather than hindsight or the officer's subjective intent.
A summary-judgment order that determines only whether the evidence presents a genuine factual dispute in a qualified-immunity case is not immediately appealable under the collateral-order doctrine.

authorities.citation: Barricks v. Wright, No. 25-1250 (4th Cir. Mar. 3, 2026)
authorities.proposition: On an interlocutory appeal from a qualified-immunity denial, the court lacks jurisdiction to revisit the district court's evidence-sufficiency assessment but may decide the legal immunity question after accepting the plaintiff-favorable facts identified below.

authorities.citation: Barricks v. Wright, No. 25-1250 (4th Cir. Mar. 3, 2026)
authorities.proposition: Accepting plaintiff-favorable facts, force must be evaluated against offense severity, immediate threat, resistance, flight, and materially changing circumstances; preexisting Fourth Circuit decisions can clearly establish that gratuitous injurious force against a surrendered or nonthreatening person is forbidden.

authorities.citation: Estate of Armstrong ex rel. Armstrong v. Village of Pinehurst, 810 F.3d 892 (4th Cir. 2016)
authorities.proposition: Resistance is not synonymous with immediate danger. Serious force such as a conducted-energy weapon must be proportionate to a reasonably perceived safety risk, including during a protective mental-health seizure involving a stationary and nonviolent person.

authorities.citation: Estate of Armstrong ex rel. Armstrong v. Village of Pinehurst, 810 F.3d 892 (4th Cir. 2016)
authorities.proposition: Although the Armstrong officers received qualified immunity for their 2011 conduct, the published decision gave later officers prospective notice that serious electrical force is disproportionate when resistance poses no immediate danger; application still turns on the specific assumed facts and force magnitude.

Viewing the facts for the plaintiff, an officer could not convert a nonviolent encounter and a person's slight, frightened resistance to an officer's initial aggression into justification for throwing her down, driving a knee into her back, and wrenching her arm; the unlawfulness was clearly established despite factual differences from prior cases.

authorities.citation: Meyers v. Baltimore County, 713 F.3d 723 (4th Cir. 2013)
authorities.proposition: Even when initial conducted-energy-weapon uses reasonably answer an armed and actively resisting threat, additional shocks become excessive after the subject is disarmed, surrounded, no longer actively resisting, and no longer poses a continuing safety threat.

It was clearly established that an officer may not repeatedly tase a nonviolent misdemeanant who is compliant, not actively resisting, and poses no safety threat; minor noncompliance does not automatically justify escalating electrical force.

Clearly established law requires precedent addressing sufficiently similar conduct with a high degree of specificity; a repeatedly warned, routine wristlock used to move a resistant protester did not become clearly unlawful from precedent addressing materially more aggressive conduct. Zorn postdates the February 3, 2025 Ellison encounter and therefore cannot itself supply notice at that time.
